Notes: First Jews in Tula were cantonists sent to the Tula arms factory in the 1830s ('Первыми евреями здесь были кантонисты (1830-е годы)'); year = midpoint of the decade

Community history began with arrival of first Jewish recruits at the arms factory in the 1830s; individual Jews lived in Tula guberniya (not necessarily the town) already in the 18th century; year = midpoint of 1830s
Jewish prayer house existed in the city by 1850
First mention of a Jewish prayer house in Tula ca. 1850; 200-300 Jewish lower-rank soldiers then served at the arms factory and military units (military subset, not total population)
'By the mid-19th century more than 300 Jews were registered at the arms factory' (arms-factory subset; year = mid-19th century approx.)
Land for a Jewish cemetery beyond Chulkovskaya sloboda approved by the arms factory commander on 24 June 1858
Meir Zafren elected rabbi in 1859; the Tula Jewish community then numbered about 500 people
A Jewish (Judaic) community appears in Tula in 1860; M. I. Zafren becomes its spiritual leader on 1 December
Meir Zafren confirmed as first official rabbi of Tula by the arms factory command in 1860; three prayer houses by 1917

1897 census, city of Tula: 2240 persons with Yiddish ('Еврейский') as native language (1265 m, 975 f); language count, religion-based figure is 2334 (see other rows)
1897 census, whole Tula guberniya (regional aggregate): 2761 Yiddish native speakers
'The 1897 census recorded more than two thousand Jews in Tula guberniya' (regional aggregate)

'By the beginning of the [20th] century the community officially numbered about 3.5 thousand' (site text reads '2-го века', evidently 20th century); 3 prayer houses, 2 Talmud Torahs, hadarim, mikvaot, cemetery, Chevra Kadisha; year = 1900 approx.
Two officially existing prayer houses in 1904 (founded 1874 and 1903)
In 1914, 3 214 persons professing Judaism lived in the city of Tula
Three synagogues functioned in 1917 (two in the centre, one in Zarechye)
1917 census sample of 4362 residents included 109 Jews (sample, not total)
Tula committee for aid to needy Jews ('Tulevpom') operated 1925-1931
House of culture of Jewish workers opened in the former synagogue building in 1928
By 1930 all Jewish property in Tula, primarily synagogues, was destroyed/confiscated; 7 Torah scrolls preserved, private gatherings continued
Efforts to register a religious community from the late 1940s succeeded only in 1988
Tula regional Jewish charity centre 'Hasdei Neshama' registered 26 April 1996; Hesed opened 29 Nov 1997
3,000-strong Jewish community in a city of 600,000; ~80% intermarried; 100-120 emigrate to Israel yearly; three synagogues closed in early Soviet decades
3,000-strong Jewish community; many members migrated from Ukraine and Belarus after WWII
Tula Jewish community officially registered 31 March 2000
Jewish community centre and synagogue opened in 2004
FJC data 2016: 700 people officially registered in Tula oblast; about 3000 Jews in the region (oblast aggregates)
